newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel says seeks more cuts in 1997 budget.
newsitem.headline: Waigel says seeks more cuts in 1997 budget.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Monday he wanted more cuts in the 1997 budget and was determined not to pay extra federal cash to cover a hole in the state jobless benefits scheme blown by rampant unemployment.
"We need to make more cuts in all areas," he said before a meeting of deputies from his Christian Social Union (CSU) and allies from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU).

Waigel last week cleared the payment of an extra 12.5 billion marks ($8.38 billion) to cover a shortfall in jobless insurance funding this year caused by a unemployment hovering near post-war highs at just under four million.
But he said that any further handouts to the Federal Labour Office next year would have to be matched by spending cuts elsewhere if there was another shortfall in the dole scheme.
He did not elaborate, saying more negotiations were needed.

Waigel spoke at the start of a week of haggling ahead of a first reading this week of the 1997 budget, which has already been approved by the cabinet. The lower house of parliament is expected to finally pass the measure in November.
Coalition budget experts met with Waigel over the weekend and agreed to cut 1997 spending by 11 billion marks to 440 billion marks and the federal deficit to 56.5 billion marks.
The 1996 deficit, budgeted at 60 billion marks, is now seen at 70 billion marks. The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) say the 1997 deficit will be 18 billion marks larger than budgeted.
Two key coalition deputies said earlier on Monday that in addition to scrapping extra federal payments for jobless pay, more steps would be needed to squeeze spending.

"An operation like this year's, where the government had to raise an extra 12.5 billion marks for the labour market through a spending freeze and other budget cuts, cannot be repeated," said CDU budget spokesman Adolf Roth and counterpart Wolfgang Weng from from junior coalition partners the Free Democrats.

Jobs-creation programmes must be sharply cut back, state subsidies for domestic coal mining and other industries must be severely curtailed, and the government must continue to trim its own personnel, they said in a joint statement.
"There is no politically acceptable way to justify less vigilance on spending consolidation or higher borrowing," they said.

Germany and other European nations are under intense pressure to bring their budget deficits down to three percent of economic output in 1997 to qualify for the scheduled 1999 launch of the single European currency.
About 250,000 union members rallied across the country over the weekend to protest against the government savings measures, which they said would aggravate, not relieve, joblessness.

But Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl said he was sure the government's Programme for More Jobs and Growth -- an austerity package envisaging overall savings of 50 billion marks -- would have the desired effect.
"That is the whole point," Bohl told German radio on Monday. "We don't just want to save for saving's sake. We want more growth, more employment, more jobs."
